comments.author: mordae
comments.text:
Why are you asking me? You should know if you are talking to a friend or a customer. :-)

Also, I don't think your odds at nailing the copy with your process are that great. Look, you need to know the connotations. Did you stop and think about naming spaces? It really comes natural in this context. Well your choice of translation also carries some. It tends to be either e.g. 3D space or the most sterile way to say, well, physical space for rent. As in office space for rent. As opposed to say flat.

Neither of these sound very social. Nor inviting.

And I imagine this will hold across most of the languages.

I had 0731 take a look, asking it:


Give me a transcript in Czech. Just the taglines, buttons, stuff like that. Do not use site's
translation. Give me your best try. Make it absolutely totally idiomatic, non-sterile, friendly,
inviting... warm place.


And it was so-so. But it was still constricted by e.g. the spaces situation. I think that for this kind of localization work you need to give translator more to work with. As in, is the term required to be exact for technical reasons? What are the feeling you are trying to evoke in the users who encounter it? I.e. what connotations are you after?

You should definitely analyze and describe your key application terminology in this manner before you start localizing, because you've pick it to be coherent in one language (or maybe two), but you did not make your intent explicit, so the results in other languages will be legible to people who speak both the target language and your original language, but it'll feel weird. And speakers of the target language with limited experience with your original language will be super confused.

BTW I don't think this is about AI at all.

comments.author: jvalol
comments.text:
Hi mordae,

Fair point, and the answer is a friend. So: informal, ty rather than vy. Same call I made in German, where it's du.

Though for what it's worth, I wasn't asking you as a customer either. No customers here, and none planned. So I suppose that makes you an internet friend who knows Czech better than anyone else I have talked to.

The "spaces" point is worse than I would have guessed. I checked all 23: every single language took the geometric or physical-room sense. Prostor, Raum, Espace, Ruimte, Tila, Χώρος, 空间. Swedish got "Utrymme", which as I understand it is closet space. Arabic did not translate it at all.

"Space" made concise sense to me for the intent, in English. Clearly that intent lands only in English, and maybe a couple of other languages if I'm lucky. So thanks for calling it out. This is exactly the sort of thing that has me out here asking.

So it is not a Czech problem, it is a me problem, and you diagnosed it exactly. I picked "spaces" in English for what it evokes. Somewhere you can be, room for you. Then I handed translators a bare noun with none of that attached. They optimized for the dictionary because the dictionary was all I gave them.

Here is the intent for that word:

space: a place people gather around a shared interest. Should feel inhabited and joinable, somewhere there is room for you. Should not read as a rented unit, a geometric region, or storage capacity. Nothing technical depends on the word, so a warmer non-literal one is more correct here than the literal one.

Given that, what would you call it in Czech?

One more, since you named the shape of it rather than just the instance. I went looking for other words like this and "My Stream" fell the same way. Czech has it as "Můj proud"; Dutch and Swedish landed on words whose first meaning is electrical current. Same cause, an English metaphor nobody else made. So your diagnosis found more than the thing it was aimed at.

And thank you. This is one of the most useful things anyone has told me about this project, including the parts that stung.

(I promise no hard feelings. Hard feedback is usually the best kind.)

Cheers,

Jake

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text: If it is locale and not lang, will this affect date formatting or maybe even large-number formatting?

comments.author: jvalol
comments.text:
That is a great question I genuinely had not thought about. After some checking, it turns out it mostly does affect date formatting appropriate for each locale. Some gaps, still looking into it.

But yes, it does more than the strings. Dates go through a per-locale table, so it's 8/3/2026 in English, 03.08.2026 in German and Czech, 2026/8/3 in Japanese, 2026-08-03 in Swedish. Relative times ("6 hours ago") are translated with real plural forms, which is where the Arabic dual and the Czech three-way turned up bugs.

Numbers are the gap: there's no CLDR in the app, so a count renders as bare digits with no grouping separator in any language, English included. Nobody sees a wrong separator, but nobody sees a right one either. It hasn't bitten yet because the numbers are small.

Your question also caught a bug. Chinese was added a day ago and I never added it to that date table, so it was falling through to the day-first default instead of 2026/8/3. Fixed, along with a test that fails if any locale lands on that fallback by accident.

I'll be following up to find other gaps and address them. The hard problem for me is always that I don't know that language or culture or whether they use commas as separators or periods, etc.

This is the sort of problem I had serious experience with at my last job. Our Ruby currency gem hadn't been updated in 13 years, and it still treated the yen as having subunits. I didn't know yen has no cents (how could I?), that's just one of the things that had drifted in 13 years, and we shipped it and made a lot of people very angry because their numbers came out wrong.

At least in this case businesses aren't affected. We're just hoping to make the internet more playful and useful for those who, like me, love the simplicity that the internet can afford.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
Well, once you add any averages, decimal-point versus decimal-comma arrives even if you skip digit grouping.


I didn't know yen has no cents (how could I?)


How many currencies you care about? Stuff relevant to international commerce can often be found in English, e.g. in Wikipedia. Foreign exchange rate trackers can be useful for checking context, but of course there is a catch: they often have rates expressed with more granularity than the currency has (because the exchange trades fixed-size lots).

Some basics can be cross-checked by using more than one model, because mistakes-within-large-flow and mistakes-in-single-sentence-analysis have quite different distributions, and so do different providers' mistakes. (We are not talking top-notch thinking performance, Gemma, Mistral, Qwen in locally-runnable sizes should be enough for basic cross-checking). Although, style and idiomatic writing will probably suffer once you go to languages not on the Wikipedia globe.

Of course, for style you can always go the pragmatic way and accept feedback of native speakers. Outright trolling is a minor risk in such context, but it will probably not pass a quick check with whatever you use as LLM or free DeepL or a local model.

comments.author: jvalol
comments.text:
The currency stuff was a former job, not this project. No money moves through PopsicleBoat, so I'm skipping that whole category for now. That was just anecdotal experience with foreign languages / currencies.

But you're right that the separator arrives anyway, and it already has. I went looking after reading your comment: the storage meter renders "1.2 GB" through a plain float interpolation, so it shows a decimal point in every language, including the ones that want a comma. No averages required. Just a byte count divided by a gigabyte.

The cross-checking point matches what I've actually been seeing, and it lines up with your split between the two kinds of mistake. Everything that has gone wrong here has been a single word with no sentence around it. "Decline" on a friend request button came back as the noun in about ten languages, so Polish read "Spadek", a decrease. "Share" became a stake in a company. "About" became "approximately" in Finnish and Hungarian. Meanwhile the paragraphs are (mostly) fine. At least I hope. It's what my LLM is telling me.

Staying in a single session is one thing I've learned to make a point of. Flow carries enough context to disambiguate. Conversely, a lone button label carries none, and that's exactly where a second model would disagree with the first.

The other half of it is that my own tooling was reporting green while all of that was on screen. A catalog can be 100% complete and still be full of English, because "the English string is correct here" and "nobody has translated this yet" were stored the same way. I split those apart today, and the number now is 3,475 strings still showing English across 23 languages. I'd rather have that number ugly and visible than not have it. The squeaky wheel gets the grease, after all.

Native speakers are working better than anything else so far. Two people from this thread have already sent specific corrections, which is worth more than any amount of model consensus.

And I didn't have to learn dozens of languages, or hire hundreds of translators to make this kind of progress, warts can be polished, but that's kind of the story here.

Anyway, the real treasure turns out to be the friends we made along the way. :)

comments.author: jvalol
comments.text:
That matches what worked here. I didn't know about it, the LLM itself brought it up. The Chinese catalog was 1,562 strings plus 37 plural blocks, done in deterministic chunks straight from the catalog inventory, each pass skipping anything already present rather than rewriting it.

The part that bit me was not generation but coverage. I checked German, saw a good translation, and wrote "translated in all 24 languages" in a commit message. Six were. The other eighteen had the English string sitting in the catalog as its own translation, which my audit counts as a known gap rather than a failure, so everything stayed green while e.g. the button read "Choose File" in Danish.

What actually caught it was making the check deterministic instead of sampled: render each public page in all 24 languages and fail if any sentence survives verbatim from the English rendering. No heuristics, no judgement about which words look English. That test found the about page problem you spotted, and a first version of it flagged "ist ein kleines soziales Netz" as English, which was a useful lesson in its own right. Like, of all languages, I know that's not English. The hard part is that there are thousands of strings, I can't personally check them all. I do have a day job after all, haha.

But dang, it would have taken me multiple lifetimes to get even half of the site translated, or at least significant funding to hire translators.

I guess for me personally, one of the adages I try to live by is "Don't let perfect be the enemy of good".

Definitely a journey for me and a lot of learnings. And a lot of fun.

That nationalist sort of language goes diametrically against the whole point of being open to other cultures.

That worry sent me checking all of them anyway, and "all of them" grows daily right now: Russian last week, Hindi about to be deployed, Bengali and Urdu in the works. Russian says находите единомышленников, the word you handed me yourself. Ukrainian says однодумців, Swedish likasinnade. The only two that reach for «folk» are Danish and Norwegian, both in the plural folks sense, dine folk / folkene dine, not the singular a-people one. If a Dane reads that differently, and wants me to hear about it, I will.

Good to know nominative-everywhere is where you landed even inside one language. Your point about the link role surviving an unreadable label is one I hadn't credited: the carrier noun still tells you it's a space even when the name is in a script you can't read. And yes, nearly every sentence here carries at most one interpolation, so no special tricks needed.
